_source: Prices are Brandywine's own published prices (brandywinefisheries.com shop, fetched 2026-08-17). Species biology, gear types and fishery seasons are public fishery-management facts (ODFW, PFMC, IPHC, NOAA FishWatch) — general knowledge about the fishery, not claims about Brandywine. Cooking temperatures follow standard culinary practice; the 145°F figure is the FDA guideline and is stated as such wherever a lower temperature is recommended.
_season_caveat: Commercial seasons are set annually by the managing council and shift year to year. Every season string below is a typical window, and the site labels it that way — never as a guarantee of what is in the case today.
_sourcing_rule: oregon_fishery:true means this is a species landed on the Oregon coast. false means Brandywine sells it but it is not an Oregon fishery — those pages say so plainly rather than letting the Oregon-boat story imply otherwise.

species.name: Chinook Salmon
species.gear: Troll — individual hooks on a line, fish brought aboard one at a time
species.gear_why: Trolling is why a boat can ice fish this carefully. Each one comes over the rail on its own and gets handled once, rather than coming up in a net with a few tons of company.
species.season: Ocean troll openings typically run spring through early fall, with the strongest summer months from May into September
species.fat: High — the fattiest of the Pacific salmon, which is where the richness comes from
species.color: Deep orange-red, occasionally the pale ivory of a white king
species.texture: Large, soft flake that pulls apart in sheets
species.flavor: Rich and buttery, the most pronounced salmon flavor of the group
species.cook_temp: 125°F for medium-rare in the center; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: High fat makes chinook forgiving — it stays moist a few degrees past where a leaner fish would go dry. Pull it when the center is still translucent and let carryover finish it.
species.portion: 6–8 oz per person for a fillet portion
species.buying: Look for flesh that springs back, a clean cut face with no gapping between the muscle segments, and a smell like cold seawater and nothing else.
species.storage: Coldest part of the fridge on ice, cooked within two days. If it must wait longer, vacuum-seal and freeze it hard rather than letting it sit.
species.fact: Chinook is the largest Pacific salmon and the most expensive fish in the Brandywine case — $29.95 a pound, against $18.95 for coho.

species.name: Coho Salmon
species.gear: Troll
species.gear_why: Same hook-and-line handling as chinook — brought aboard one at a time and iced immediately.
species.season: Ocean coho openings are concentrated in late summer, typically peaking in August and September
species.fat: Moderate — leaner than chinook, richer than most white fish
species.color: Bright red-orange, a touch lighter than chinook
species.flavor: Clean and distinctly salmon, without chinook's heaviness
species.cook_temp: 125–130°F in the center; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: Less fat than chinook means less margin. Coho goes from perfect to chalky in about ninety seconds, so cook it hot and short and take it off early.
species.buying: A firm fillet with tight, glossy flesh. Coho fillets are smaller and thinner than chinook, so they cook faster than people expect.
species.storage: On ice in the fridge, cooked within two days.
species.fact: Coho runs $11 a pound under chinook in the Brandywine case — the same fishery, the same boat handling, at roughly two-thirds the price.

species.name: Steelhead
species.gear: Sold by Brandywine primarily in the smokehouse line — smoked and smoked peppered
species.season: Sold year-round from the smoked case rather than as a fresh seasonal item
species.color: Orange-pink, generally lighter than salmon
species.flavor: Milder and sweeter than salmon — the reason it takes smoke so well
species.cook_temp: 125–130°F if you are cooking a fresh piece; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: Brandywine sells steelhead smoked, so most of what leaves the case is ready to eat cold. Treat the peppered version as a centerpiece rather than an ingredient.
species.portion: 3–4 oz per person as smoked fish on a board
species.buying: Smoked steelhead should be glossy and firm, never sticky or weeping.
species.storage: Smoked fish keeps sealed in the fridge for a week or so; once opened, days rather than weeks.
species.fact: Smoked steelhead and smoked peppered steelhead are both $40 in the Brandywine case — $10 under the smoked salmon at $50.

species.name: Pacific Halibut
species.gear: Longline — baited hooks set along a groundline on the bottom
species.gear_why: Longline gear is selective and brings fish up individually, which is what allows the careful bleeding and icing that keeps halibut's white flesh genuinely white.
species.season: The directed commercial season is set annually by the International Pacific Halibut Commission and typically runs spring into late fall
species.fat: Very lean — among the leanest fish in the case
species.color: Bright, opaque white, almost translucent when raw
species.texture: Firm and dense with a large flake; the steak of white fish
species.flavor: Clean and mild with a faint sweetness
species.cook_temp: 130–135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: This is the easiest fish in the case to ruin. Almost no fat means nothing buffers it once the proteins tighten — the difference between excellent and dry halibut is about four degrees. Use a thermometer, not a timer.
species.portion: 6 oz per person; halibut is dense and eats larger than it looks
species.buying: Snow-white flesh with no yellowing at the edges and no gapping. A halibut steak should look like it was cut, not torn.
species.storage: Two days maximum on ice. Lean fish does not sit well.
species.fact: At $38.95 a pound, halibut is the most expensive fish Brandywine sells by weight — more than chinook salmon.

species.name: Black Cod (Sablefish)
species.gear: Longline and pot gear, fished deep
species.gear_why: Sablefish live deep — hundreds to thousands of feet down — which is why they carry the oil content they do.
species.season: Fished essentially year-round under a quota system rather than in a short seasonal window
species.fat: Very high — the highest oil content of anything in the case
species.color: Pearl white, almost luminous
species.texture: Silky, unusually large soft flake that separates into velvety sheets
species.flavor: Rich and buttery, closer to a fatty salmon than to a white fish
species.cook_temp: 140°F — this is the one fish that genuinely wants to go a little further
species.cook_note: All that oil makes black cod nearly impossible to overcook. It is the forgiving fish — if halibut intimidates you, start here.
species.portion: 5–6 oz per person; it is rich enough that people eat less of it
species.buying: Look for a bright, almost wet-looking sheen. Dull black cod has been sitting.
species.storage: The high oil content means it holds a little better than lean fish, but two to three days is still the window.
species.fact: Black cod is the same $18.95 a pound as coho and lingcod, and it is the fish most likely to convert someone who thinks they do not like fish.

species.name: Lingcod
species.gear: Hook and line, jigged over rocky nearshore ground
species.gear_why: Lingcod hold on structure, so they are fished with jigs over reef rather than dragged.
species.season: Nearshore openings typically run spring through fall, with depth restrictions that change through the year
species.color: White — and sometimes a startling blue-green that cooks out to pure white
species.texture: Firm with a large flake, meaty enough to hold together on a grill
species.flavor: Mild and slightly sweet
species.cook_temp: 135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: Firm enough for the grill and for fish tacos, which is what most of it becomes. It holds its shape better than cod or sole.
species.buying: The blue-green flesh some lingcod carry is a harmless natural pigment called biliverdin. It cooks to white. It is not a defect and it is not a sign of anything wrong.
species.storage: Two to three days on ice.
species.fact: Roughly one lingcod in five comes up with blue-green flesh. It disappears entirely in the pan.

species.name: Pacific Rockfish
species.gear: Hook and line over nearshore reef
species.gear_why: Rockfish are a structure species taken over rocky ground rather than open bottom.
species.season: Available across most of the year, with the nearshore fishery shaped by seasonal depth restrictions
species.color: White with a faint pink cast when raw
species.texture: Medium flake, tender, more delicate than lingcod
species.flavor: Mild and clean — the least assertive fish in the case
species.cook_temp: 135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: The everyday fish. Thin fillets cook in minutes, which means the pan should be hot and you should be standing there.
species.buying: "Sebastes" covers dozens of species — black, yellowtail, canary, widow, and more. They cook interchangeably.
species.storage: Two days. Delicate fillets go soft faster than firm ones.
species.fact: At $13.95 a pound, rockfish is the least expensive fresh fish Brandywine sells — and the one most likely to end up in a fish taco.

species.name: Pacific Cod
species.price: Ask at the counter — availability varies
species.gear: Hook and line and trawl gear
species.season: A cold-water fishery, strongest in the winter and spring months
species.color: Bright white
species.texture: Large, tender flake that breaks apart easily
species.flavor: Mild, clean, faintly sweet
species.cook_temp: 135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: The classic fish-and-chips fish. The big tender flake that makes it good battered is the same thing that makes it fall apart on a grill — keep it in a pan or in oil.
species.buying: Cod should look bright and wet, never chalky.
species.storage: Two days. Cod is among the more perishable white fish.
species.fact: Brandywine keeps a Pacific Cod section in its recipe library — it is a staple of the case rather than a specialty item.

species.name: Sole and Flounder
species.price: Ask at the counter — availability varies
species.gear: Trawl gear on soft bottom
species.season: Landed across much of the year; petrale is at its best in the cooler months
species.color: White, thin fillets
species.texture: Fine, delicate flake — the most fragile fish in the case
species.flavor: Delicate and sweet
species.cook_temp: 135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: Thin fillets cook in two or three minutes a side. Flour, hot butter, lemon, done — anything more elaborate tends to destroy it.
species.portion: 8 oz per person; sole fillets are thin and light
species.buying: Petrale is the prized one of the group and the one most often asked for by name.
species.storage: One to two days. Thin, lean fillets have the shortest life of anything here.
species.fact: Brandywine groups halibut, sole and flounder together in its recipe library — they are all flatfish and they all cook by the same rules.

species.name: Albacore Tuna
species.price: Canned from $12.00; smoked loin $40.00 / lb, $20.00 / half lb
species.gear: Troll and jig gear
species.gear_why: Oregon's albacore fleet trolls barbless jigs — fish come aboard one at a time, which is the same handling story as the salmon.
species.season: Albacore move into range off the Oregon coast in the warm-water months, typically July through October
species.color: Pale pink to ivory — the palest tuna
species.flavor: Mild for a tuna, clean, without the iron note of the red tunas
species.cook_temp: Sear the outside and leave the middle rare — 115–120°F in the center
species.cook_note: Cooked through, albacore turns dry and grainy. If you want it cooked all the way, buy the canned version, which is packed for exactly that.
species.buying: Brandywine's canned albacore comes in All Natural, Alderwood Smoked, and Jalapeño — $12, $15 and $13 a tin respectively, with case pricing up to $330.
species.storage: Fresh loin, two days. Canned, years.
species.fact: The canned albacore is the item most associated with the brand — it is one of the eight things the Springfield store lists as always in stock.

species.name: Ahi (Yellowfin) Tuna
species.sourcing: Yellowfin is a warm-water tuna and is not an Oregon fishery. Brandywine sells it alongside the Oregon catch — it is bought in, not landed by the boat.
species.gear: Not applicable — sourced rather than landed by the Brandywine
species.season: Available year-round as a sourced item
species.color: Deep red, the classic tuna color
species.flavor: Clean and mild, with more of a tuna edge than albacore
species.cook_temp: Rare — 115°F in the center, or served raw
species.cook_note: Ahi is a searing fish. Thirty seconds a side on a very hot pan, sliced against the grain.
species.buying: At $8.95 this is one of the lowest-priced items on the fresh list.
species.storage: Two days, cold.
species.fact: Ahi and albacore are both tuna and they behave completely differently in a pan. Ahi wants to stay red; albacore wants to stay pink.

species.name: Swordfish
species.sourcing: Not an Oregon nearshore fishery. Brandywine carries swordfish steaks as a sourced item alongside the boat's own catch.
species.gear: Not applicable — sourced rather than landed by the Brandywine
species.season: Available as a sourced item rather than on an Oregon season
species.color: Ivory to pale pink
species.texture: Very firm and dense — the most steak-like fish sold
species.flavor: Mild and slightly sweet, meatier than any other fish in the case
species.cook_temp: 130–135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: Swordfish is thick and dense, so it takes real grill time — and it dries out badly once it goes past. Thick steaks, high heat, thermometer.
species.buying: Look for a steak with a tight, moist grain and no brown streaking.
species.storage: Two to three days.
species.fact: Brandywine keeps swordfish and mahi mahi together in one recipe category — both are firm, both grill, both are sourced rather than Oregon-landed.

species.name: Mahi Mahi
species.sourcing: A tropical and subtropical species — not an Oregon fishery. Carried as a sourced item.
species.gear: Not applicable — sourced rather than landed by the Brandywine
species.season: Available as a sourced item year-round
species.color: Pinkish when raw, cooking to white
species.flavor: Mild and sweet
species.cook_temp: 135°F; the FDA guideline is 145°F
species.cook_note: Firm enough to grill without falling apart, which is most of its appeal. Lean enough that it wants a marinade or a sauce.
species.buying: At $9.95 it sits near the bottom of the fresh price list.
species.storage: Two to three days.
species.fact: Mahi mahi is not related to dolphins in any way — the old name 'dolphinfish' causes more confusion at fish counters than any other name in the trade.

species.name: Dungeness Crab
species.gear: Baited pots set on sand and mud bottom
species.season: Oregon's commercial season traditionally opens in December and runs into the following summer, with the opening date set each year on meat-fill and toxin testing
species.color: Orange-red shell when cooked, white meat
species.flavor: Sweet and briny — Oregon's signature shellfish
species.cook_temp: Boiled or steamed until hot through; most crab is sold already cooked
species.cook_note: Most Dungeness leaves a counter already cooked. The job at home is reheating gently or not at all — cold cracked crab is the point.
species.portion: One whole crab per person, or 1/2 lb of picked meat
species.buying: Crab is one of the eight items the Springfield store lists as always carried.
species.storage: Cooked crab keeps two days cold. Picked meat, less.
species.fact: The Oregon Dungeness season opening is delayed most years until the crab test full on meat content — the fishery waits for the crab rather than the calendar.

species.name: Bay Shrimp
species.gear: Trawl gear fitted with excluder devices
species.gear_why: Oregon's pink shrimp fishery is one of the most-cited bycatch-reduction success stories on the West Coast — the fleet uses excluders and LED lighting to keep finfish out of the net.
species.season: The Oregon pink shrimp season runs from spring into late fall, typically April through October
species.color: Pale pink, cooked
species.flavor: Sweet and mild
species.cook_temp: Already cooked when sold — no further cooking needed
species.cook_note: Bay shrimp come cooked and peeled. Heating them is almost always a mistake; they go rubbery in seconds. Fold them into things cold.
species.portion: 4 oz per person in a salad or roll
species.buying: At $9.00 these are the cheapest shellfish on the list.
species.storage: Two days cold. They are already cooked, which shortens rather than lengthens the window.
species.fact: Oregon's pink shrimp fishery has been certified sustainable and is regularly held up as a model for how trawl gear can be modified to nearly eliminate bycatch.

species.name: Raw Shrimp
species.sourcing: Large raw shrimp are not an Oregon fishery. These are a sourced item, separate from the Oregon bay shrimp.
species.gear: Not applicable — sourced
species.season: Available year-round as a sourced item
species.color: Grey-translucent raw, pink cooked
species.flavor: Sweet and clean
species.cook_temp: Cook just until opaque and curled into a loose C
species.cook_note: A shrimp curled into a tight O is overcooked. A loose C is right. That is the whole technique.
species.buying: The numbers are counts per pound — 13/15 means thirteen to fifteen shrimp make a pound, so they are larger than the 16/20. Bigger count number, smaller shrimp.
species.storage: Raw shrimp, two days cold.
species.fact: The $5 difference between 13/15 and 16/20 buys you noticeably larger shrimp — about 20% more meat per piece.

species.name: Fresh Oysters
species.gear: Farmed on Oregon's estuaries and bays
species.season: Available year-round; oysters are firmest and best in the cold months
species.color: Grey-cream
species.flavor: Briny, cucumber-sweet, with a mineral finish that changes by growing bay
species.cook_temp: Raw on the half shell, or grilled just until the shells pop open
species.cook_note: The old rule about months with an R in them is a spawning-season quality rule, not a safety rule — farmed oysters are sold safely year-round.
species.portion: 6 oysters per person as a starter
species.buying: Fresh oysters are one of the eight items the Springfield store lists as always carried — and one of the things that does not travel to a market booth.
species.storage: Cup-side down, covered with a damp cloth, never sealed in a bag or in water. They are alive and they need air.
species.fact: The Springfield store is the only Brandywine counter that carries fresh oysters — they do not go to the farmers market booths.

species.name: Black Mussels
species.gear: Rope-grown
species.season: Available year-round
species.color: Orange-cream meat in a blue-black shell
species.flavor: Sweet and briny
species.cook_temp: Steam just until the shells open, three to five minutes
species.cook_note: Discard any that stay shut after steaming. Before cooking, tap any open ones — if they close, they are alive and fine.
species.portion: 1 lb per person as a main
species.buying: At $6.95 mussels are the least expensive item in the entire Brandywine case.
species.storage: In the fridge under a damp cloth, never sealed or submerged. Cook within a day or two.
species.fact: Mussels are the cheapest thing Brandywine sells and one of the fastest — a pound goes from bag to bowl in about five minutes.

species.name: Steamer Clams
species.gear: Harvested from Oregon's tideflats and bays
species.season: Available year-round
species.color: Cream meat, tan-striped shell
species.flavor: Sweet and strongly briny
species.cook_temp: Steam until the shells open, five minutes or so
species.cook_note: Brandywine sells these already prepared in garlic butter, which means the work is done — heat and serve with bread.
species.buying: Sold as a prepared item in garlic butter at $8.95, alongside the crab cakes at $9.95.
species.storage: Cold, under a damp cloth, cooked within a day or two.
species.fact: Steamer clams in garlic butter and crab cakes are two of only three items in Brandywine's prepared-seafood case.

species.name: Scallops
species.sourcing: Not an Oregon fishery. Carried as a sourced item — Brandywine sells them primarily out of the smokehouse line.
species.gear: Not applicable — sourced
species.season: Available year-round
species.color: Ivory to pale cream
species.flavor: Sweet and rich
species.cook_temp: Sear hard and fast — the center should stay just translucent
species.cook_note: Dry the scallop thoroughly before it hits the pan. Wet scallops steam instead of searing, and a steamed scallop is a sad thing.
species.buying: Scallops are one of the eight items the Springfield store lists as always carried.
species.storage: Two days cold on a rack over ice, not sitting in liquid.
species.fact: Brandywine's smoked scallops are $20 — the least expensive item in the thirteen-piece smoked line after the smoked oysters at $15.
